# Pseudomonas aeruginosa relies on a phosphoketolase to support anaerobic survival under reductive stress

**Authors:** Richard D. Horak; Nanqing Zhou; Korbinian O. Thalhammer; Nathan F. Dalleska; Ludmilla Aristilde; Dianne K. Newman

**Affiliations:** (1)Division of Biology and Biological Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, United States | (2)Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, McCormick School of Engineering and Applied Science, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL 60208, United States | (3)Division of Geological and Planetary Sciences, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, United States | (4)Northwestern Center for Synthetic Biology, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL 60208, United States | (5)Water and Environment Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, United States

## Abstract

Across diverse contexts, bacteria experience loss of electron acceptors due to fluctuating environmental conditions, leading to growth-arrest and reductive stress. Yet, microbial metabolism has been primarily studied with cells growing under nutrient replete conditions. To study how cells preserve metabolic flux under reductively stressed growth-arrest, we explored how the opportunistic pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa remodels its metabolism under such conditions. During anaerobic survival on glucose, P. aeruginosa utilizes the upper Embden-Meyerhoff-Parnas pathway and pentose-phosphate pathway to generate metabolite precursors for a previously undescribed phosphoketolase (herein termed xfp) used to produce acetyl-P and indirectly ATP via subsequent acetate formation. This re-routing bypasses P. aeruginosa’s canonical glucose-catabolizing Entner-Doudoroff pathway (EDP) allowing for metabolic flux without exacerbating reductive stress. Moreover, anaerobic survival on diverse carbon sources triggers purine degradation and metabolite accumulation, requiring xfp to maintain metabolic balance and viability. Thus, our data suggest that phosphoketolases may play an additional role in ribonucleotide balance. This study expands our understanding of P. aeruginosa’s anaerobic survival strategies and serves as a reminder that large gaps remain in our understanding of growth arrest physiology even in well-studied model organisms, highlighting the potential for basic discovery in the realm of non-growth metabolism.

## Introduction

Despite the immense diversity of metabolic strategies across the tree of life, the rules underpinning them are remarkably unified. All life must couple energy generation with energy expenditures (e.g. biosynthesis); a process accomplished via carefully managed redox reactions (Chubukov et al., 2014). Loss of redox balance, such as an inability to consume excess reducing equivalents (i.e. reductive stress), leads to metabolic disruption, growth arrest, and even cellular death (Xiao and Loscalzo, 2020). From the perspective of human biology, reductive stress is commonly thought to be purely detrimental due to its linkage to a variety of illnesses (Cantó, Menzies and Auwerx, 2015; Luo, Ma and Ye, 2024; Ying, 2008; Yang, Guo and Li, 2025). Yet, microorganisms are commonly found in oxidant-limited environments, such as in bioreactors, soil communities, and human infections (Silver, Lugo and Keller, 1999; Enfors et al., 2001; Cowley et al., 2015; Voroney and Heck, 2015; Bergkessel, Basta and Newman, 2016). While numerous studies have uncovered diverse fermentative metabolisms to support growth under reductive stress (Bartacek, Zabranska and Lens, 2007; Hackmann and Zhang, 2023; Hackmann, 2024; Thauer, Jungermann and Decker, 1977), we know far less about the metabolic strategies supporting growth-arrested survival in bacteria reliant on respiration for growth.

Within the metabolism field, a historic focus on bacterial growth has led to many organisms being defined as “non-fermentative” or “obligate aerobes” based on their inability to grow under oxidant-limited conditions. Yet many of these bacteria contain fermentation genes. For example, in the traditionally deemed “obligate aerobe” Mycobacterium smegmatis, cells can utilize fermentative hydrogen production to alleviate reductive stress and generate ATP during hypoxia-induced growth arrest (Berney et al., 2014). A related phenomenon is observed in human biology, with hypoxia and mitochondrial dysfunction stimulating the Warburg effect, whereby glycolysis outpaces respiration leading to lactate production to consume excess reducing equivalents while maintaining ATP production (Warburg, 1925; Kukurugya, Rosset and Titov, 2024). Because bacteria that rely on aerobic respiration for growth can be challenged by oxygen limitation (Ciemniecki and Newman, 2020; Silver, Lugo and Keller, 1999; Voroney and Heck, 2015), it is likely that these fermentative strategies to support non-growth survival in respiratory organisms may be more common than has been realized.

An alternative to consuming reducing equivalents to maintain metabolic flux under reductive stress is to use metabolic pathways that do not generate reducing equivalents. To test this idea, we turned to the “non-fermentative” pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa, known to survive for weeks in oxidant-limited growth-arrested states, herein termed “anaerobic survival” (Eschbach et al., 2004). P. aeruginosa depends on respiration of molecular oxygen or via denitrification to support exponential growth (Gayon and Dupetit, 1886; Zumft, 1997); it is unable to grow exponentially in the absence of terminal electron acceptors. However, it can metabolize arginine and yeast extract for slight anaerobic growth or ferment pyruvate to support anaerobic survival (Vander Wauven et al., 1984). In the case of the latter, pyruvate is metabolized to acetate via acetyl-CoA and acetyl-phosphate (acetyl-P) by the ackA-pta system, generating ATP and NADH. Meanwhile, generation of lactate from additional pyruvate molecules via ldhA regenerates NAD+ (Eschbach et al., 2004) (FIG 1A).

On carbon sources such as glucose, P. aeruginosa also relies on ackA-pta for ATP generation and can persist in a non-growth state (Ciemniecki et al., 2024; Glasser, Kern and Newman, 2014). However, glucose-surviving cells can only survive if they employ phenazines – self-made electron shuttles – to alleviate reductive stress (Ciemniecki et al., 2024; Glasser, Kern and Newman, 2014). P. aeruginosa lacks a complete upper Embden-Meyerhoff-Parnas pathway (EMPP) for standard glycolysis and lacks the oxidative pentose-phosphate pathway (PPP) (Kohlstedt and Wittmann, 2019; Lessie and Phibbs, 1984). During aerobic growth, almost all glucose catabolic flux occurs first via oxidation of glucose to gluconate, followed by further oxidation or its phosphorylation, eventually generating 6-phosphogluconate that feeds into the Entner-Doudoroff pathway (EDP) and lower EMPP (Kohlstedt and Wittmann, 2019). However, during anaerobic survival this glycolytic pathway would generate excess reducing equivalents ([2e-]) via reduced ubiquinone from initial glucose oxidation, and NADPH or NADH from the lower EMPP (FIG 1A). Therefore, we predicted that under reductive stress P. aeruginosa’s glucose catabolic flux would shift towards the non-oxidative upper EMPP and PPP by way of glucose-6-phosphate (glucose-6P) and fructose-6-phosphate (fructose-6P).

Precedent for such metabolic re-routing in P. aeruginosa exists in the literature. Despite catabolizing glucose to gluconate during aerobic growth (generating reduced ubiquinone), during anaerobic growth on nitrate as a terminal electron acceptor, P. aeruginosa instead catabolized all measurable glucose to glucose-6P (Lessie and Phibbs, 1984). However, use of the lower EMPP to connect the PPP to acetate and ATP production would still generate excess reducing equivalents, unless paired with lactate production, limiting ATP and acetate yields (Fig 1A). An alternative non-oxidative path connecting the PPP to acetate production is via phosphoketolases, one such protein being previously discovered and purified from P. aeruginosa ATCC 15442 (Petrareanu et al., 2014).

Phosphoketolases are thiamine-pyrophosphate-dependent enzymes that catalyze the phosphorolysis of fructose-6-phosphate (fructose-6P), xylulose-5-phosphate (xylulose-5P), and/or sedoheptulose-7-phosphate (sedoheptulose-7P), releasing 2 carbons from each substrate as acetyl-P and generating erythrose-4-phosphate (erythrose-4P), glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (glyceraldehyde-3P), or ribose-5-phosphate (ribose-5P), respectively (Krüsemann et al., 2018; Sánchez et al., 2010; Suzuki et al., 2010). The activity and preference for each substrate differs across phosphoketolase homologs in different species. Phosphoketolases have been primarily studied for their role in natural product generation and in fermentative metabolisms such as hexose catabolism via the phosphoketolase pathway in some Lactobacillus species and the bifido-shunt in Bifidobacterium species, as well as pentose catabolism in Clostridium acetobutylicum (Aristilde et al., 2015; Årsköld et al., 2008; de Vries and Stouthamer, 1967; Liu et al., 2012). Within C. acetobutylicum, phosphoketolases provide efficient non-oxidative pentose catabolism while supporting ATP generation. This metabolism bypasses pentose flux through the PPP or EMPP, avoiding rate-limiting enzymatic steps, carbon loss, and generation of additional reducing equivalents (Aristilde et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2012; Servinsky et al., 2012). During energy-limited anaerobic survival in P. aeruginosa, a similar strategy would allow for continued ATP production while minimizing protein cost and reducing equivalent generation (FIG 1A). While P. aeruginosa contains many of the genes involved in the bifido-shunt, it is unable to consume excess reducing equivalents via ethanol generation through the enzyme ethanol dehydrogenase.

Intriguingly, the phosphoketolase gene of P. aeruginosa is regulated by the anaerobic transcription factor Anr and its regulatory small RNA esrA, indicating a potential role for phosphoketolases during anaerobic carbon metabolism in this organism (Ferrara et al., 2021; Hammond et al., 2015; Tribelli et al., 2019). Accordingly, we set out to test the hypothesis that during anaerobic survival on glucose, metabolic flux diverts into the non-oxidative PPP, enabling Xfp to utilize PPP metabolites, such as xylulose-5P, to form acetyl-P, ultimately leading to acetate and ATP production, while avoiding additional production of reducing equivalents (FIG 1A).

## Results

### P. aeruginosa relies on a phosphoketolase during anaerobic survival on glucose under reductive stress

Evidence in support of our hypothesis, that during anaerobic survival P. aeruginosa catabolizes glucose via the non-oxidative PPP and a putative phosphoketolase, came from a preliminary transposon-sequencing (Tn-seq) screen performed in our lab using P. aeruginosa UCBPP-PA14 (PA14) surviving anaerobically on glucose in the presence of phenazine-1-carboxylic acid (Saunders, 2020). Despite PA14 relying on the EDP for aerobic glucose catabolism, transposon insertions in the core EDP gene edaA, catalyzing the formation of glyceraldehyde-3P and pyruvate, or in the positive EDP regulator hexR, increased survival on glucose (FIG 1A) (Saunders, 2020). Meanwhile, transposon insertion in genes involved in the upper EMPP, the PPP gene transaldolase, the ackA-pta system, or a putative phosphoketolase (PA14_17580, here-in referred to as xfp), were all detrimental to PA14’s survival (FIG 1A) (Saunders, 2020). While PA14’s Xfp has not been purified and confirmed for phosphoketolase activity, its amino acid sequence is nearly identical to the previously purified phosphoketolase of P. aeruginosa strain ATCC 15442, with only two amino acid identities differing (SUPP FIG1). The Xfp of 15442 was confirmed to have in vitro enzymatic activity on both fructose-6P and xylulose-5P, with a strong preference for the latter (Petrareanu et al., 2014). Therefore, we reasoned that PA14’s Xfp might retain this catalytic capability, preferentially consuming xylulose-5P to generate glyceraldehyde-3P and acetyl-P, bridging the non-oxidative PPP and acetate generation to support anaerobic survival and ATP production on glucose.

To determine whether the loss of xfp results in a survival deficit during reductively stressed anaerobic survival on glucose, we generated a clean deletion of PA14_17580. All experiments were performed in a phenazine-null mutant background (Δphz) to avoid alleviation of reductive stress by phenazines and better isolate a Xfp-dependent reductive stress survival mechanism. To test for survival, anoxic cell suspensions of Δphz and ΔphzΔxfp strains were sampled and plated for colony-forming units (CFUs) over time. Both strains maintained ~100% survival for the first 3 days of anaerobic survival, yet by day 5, ΔphzΔxfp CFUs dropped over 2 orders of magnitude, before plateauing between 10 and 15 days (FIG 1B). Meanwhile the parent strain Δphz maintained ~100% survival for 10 days before losing viability, plateauing to a similar level as the xfp mutant – 2 orders of magnitude lower than starting CFUs (FIG 1B). Complementation of xfp in the ΔphzΔxfp strain fully restored viability (SUPP FIG 2A). Additionally, there was no effect of the xfp mutation during anaerobic growth on glucose using KNO3 as a terminal electron acceptor (SUPP FIG 2B). Finally, to confirm this effect was not due to the Δphz background, we additionally generated a Δxfp strain in the WT PA14 background, observing no statistical difference between it and the ΔphzΔxfp strain (SUPP FIG 2A).

To test our assumption that Xfp is only needed under conditions of reductive-stress, we repeated the experiment above in a 96-well plate equipped with electrodes, allowing us to determine if the addition of phenazines could rescue the ΔphzΔxfp strain. Cells were given 200 μM, 50 μM, or 0 μM of phenazine-1-carboximide (PCN), an endogenous electron shuttle produced by PA14. Each well of the 96-well plate contained a working, reference, and counter electrode, enabling any PCN that is reduced by cells to be re-oxidized at the working electrode, allowing for dissipation of reducing equivalents. In support of our hypothesis that reductive stress causes the need for Xfp to maintain viability, we see that 200 μM of PCN rescues the survival of the ΔphzΔxfp strain (Fig 1C). Notably, the Δphz strain is unable to maintain 100% survival in the absence of PCN, yet 50 μM is enough to promote full viability. However, the ΔphzΔxfp strain still dies in the presence of 50 μM PCN, suggesting a greater demand for an electron acceptor to restore redox balance in the xfp mutant (Fig 1C). Together, these data suggests that Xfp and phenazines play complementary roles in allowing cells to maintain survival under reductive stress.

### P. aeruginosa utilizes a phosphoketolase-mediated pathway for catabolism of glucose to acetate during anaerobic survival

To verify that PA14 can use its Xfp for glucose catabolism and acetate production, we performed pathway-diagnostic isotopic labelling experiments. Both Δphz and ΔphzΔxfp strains were incubated with 1-13C1-glucose and supernatants were removed on days 3/5/7 for the Δphz strain and on day 3 for ΔphzΔxfp. We then measured the relative abundance of acetate and the fraction that was 13C labelled. PA14 relies on ackA-mediated ATP generation during anaerobic survival on glucose. Accordingly, if all 1-13C1-glucose is catabolized via the EDP and lower EMPP to form pyruvate and then acetate via ackA-pta, we expected all acetate would lack 13C labelling due to loss of 13C as CO2 during formation of acetyl-CoA (FIG 2A). However, if 1-13C1-glucose were instead catabolized via a bifido-shunt-like phosphoketolase-mediated metabolism, we predicted a fraction of the acetate would be 13C labelled, specifically at the first carbon atom. As PA14 lacks the oxidative PPP, this latter possibility would require glucose to enter the PPP by way of glucose-6P and fructose-6P, where 13C labelled fructose-6P is either directly processed by Xfp, or interconverted to xylulose-5P and/or sedoheptulose-7P, potential Xfp substrates. Cleavage of any of these three potential substrates by Xfp would thus be expected to release singly 13C-labelled acetyl-P, which can then form acetate via ackA or acetyl-CoA via pta, all of which would be 13C labelled in the first position (FIG 2A). However, the strong homology of PA14’s Xfp to a previously purified P. aeruginosa phosphoketolase (Petrareanu et al., 2014, SUPP FIG1) suggests a preference for xylulose-5P as a substrate, generating glyceraldehyde-3P and acetyl-P as products, denoted by red boxes in Figure 2A.

By day 3 of anaerobic survival, we observed no significant 13C labelling of acetate from ΔphzΔxfp supernatants, meanwhile, ~20% of acetate from Δphz samples was singly 13C labelled, increasing to ~40% by day 7 (FIG 2B). Additionally, by day 3, Δphz supernatants contained around twice the acetate of ΔphzΔxfp supernatants (FIG 2C). While acetate was primarily visible as the acetic acid molecular ion (CH3COOH+), in-source fragmentation also allowed detection of the second carbon atom in the form of carboxylic acid cations (HCO2+). Despite high levels of singly labelled acetate in Δphz supernatants, we were unable to detect substantial doubly 13C labelled acetic acid or singly 13C labelled carboxylic acid fragments. Taken together, these results indicate that acetate produced by Δphz cells from 1-13C1-glucose is singly 13C labelled at the methyl position. It is important to note that the fraction of 13C labelled-acetate likely underestimates the contribution of Xfp to acetate generation, as Xfp substrates can also be generated from unlabeled endogenous carbon stores, or unlabeled glucose-derived fructose-6P or glyceraldehyde-3P. Regardless, these findings demonstrate that during anaerobic survival on glucose, PA14 can utilize an alternative glucose catabolic pathway for acetate production.

### P. aeruginosa relies on Xfp for metabolic homeostasis of endogenous metabolites during anaerobic survival on glucose

Having established that PA14 can utilize a PPP and Xfp-mediated metabolism for acetate generation during anaerobic survival on glucose, we were curious whether Xfp played any additional roles in metabolic homeostasis. To test this, we repeated our anaerobic survival experiments, using the Δphz and ΔphzΔxfp strains, as well as a ΔphzΔackAΔpta strain – unable to generate acetate or acetyl-CoA from acetyl-P – and a ΔphzΔackAΔptaΔxfp strain. Loss of ackA-pta is less detrimental than loss of xfp and loss of all three genes is as detrimental as loss of xfp alone (Fig 3A). This suggests that both acetate and acetyl-CoA generation from Xfp-derived acetyl-P is dispensable early in survival, implying that Xfp plays an additional role under these conditions.

To identify this role, we repeated our 1-13C1-glucose experiment with the Δphz and ΔphzΔxfp strains, extracting intracellular metabolites and measuring their relative abundance and fraction of 13C isotopic incorporation. On day 3, 60–80% of glucose-6P, fructose-6P and sedoheptulose-7P were 13C labelled in the Δphz strain, consistent with flux of glucose into the upper EMPP and PPP. However, in the ΔphzΔxfp strain we observed only 20–40% 13C incorporation for these same metabolites (Fig 3B). Despite lower 13C labelling in ΔphzΔxfp cells, upper EMPP and PPP metabolites were ~4–8 times higher than in Δphz cells (Fig 3C). The simultaneous low 13C labelling of PPP-metabolites and ~4–8 times increase in their abundance in ΔphzΔxfp cells suggests input into the PPP, from glucose or endogenous carbon stores, outpaces PPP metabolite consumption. Additionally, as the increase in metabolite abundance is larger than the decrease in 13C labelling for metabolites such as sedoheptulose-7P, these results may suggest that 13C incorporation and PPP influx is faster in ΔphzΔxfp cells than Δphz cells for some metabolites.

As 13C labelling of upper EMPP and PPP metabolites continued to increase by a few percent in the Δphz strain across the 7 days (SUPP FIG 3A/3B), we noted a decrease in the relative abundance of these metabolites by half (SUPP FIG 3C). The presence of doubly and triply 13C labelled ribose-5P and sedoheptulose-7P in Δphz cells throughout survival suggests substantial cycling of glucose-derived metabolites through the PPP (FIG 2B, SUPP FIG 3B). The lack of detection of acetyl-CoA, absence of significant 13C labelling of TCA cycle metabolites, and lack of detection of 13C labelling of N-acetyl-glutamate, despite its significant consumption in Δphz cells throughout survival, leaves us unable to determine if any Xfp-derived acetyl-P is used to form acetyl-CoA (SUPP FIG 3A/3C/3D). Meanwhile a lack of pyruvate 13C labelling, despite little change in its abundance over 7 days in Δphz cells suggests little flux out of the EDP (Fig 2B). However, EDP metabolites were undetectable so we cannot comment on levels of flux into the EDP.

To determine which metabolite differences were caused by anaerobic survival or xfp loss per se, we compared metabolite abundance in cells before and after the start of our survival experiment. Before anaerobic survival, the ΔphzΔxfp strain showed no dramatic differences in PPP metabolites compared to the Δphz strain, and though we observed some differences between the strains, such as 1.5-log decrease decrease in phenylalanine levels in ΔphzΔxfp cells, these differences were largely abolished after 3 days of anaerobic survival on glucose (SUPP FIG 4A/4B). Both strains individually showed an increase of up to 5-fold of upper EMPP, PPP, and TCA cycle metabolites during anaerobic survival compared to their levels beforehand, likely due to lower carbon utilization rates during growth arrest (FIG 3D/3E, SUPP FIG 4C/4D). These results indicate that anaerobic survival itself causes widespread central carbon metabolite accumulation, but that Xfp is important for balancing metabolite influx and consumption, specifically in the upper EMPP and PPP.

### P. aeruginosa’s Xfp maintains metabolic homeostasis and viability during anaerobic survival on diverse carbon sources and in the absence of exogenous carbon

The accumulation of unlabeled EMPP and PPP metabolites in ΔphzΔxfp cells from presumptive metabolism of endogenous carbon stores suggested that the ΔphzΔxfp strain might exhibit similar phenotypes when provided with carbon sources other than glucose. Accordingly, we repeated our survival experiments on a variety of carbon sources or the absence of an exogenous carbon source. By Day 7 of anaerobic survival the ΔphzΔxfp mutant showed over 10-fold lower CFUs on all carbon sources except for pyruvate, as well as in the no carbon condition (Fig 4A). Additionally, by day 3, we observed mean metabolite levels of upper EMPP and PPP ~2 to 16 times higher in the ΔphzΔxfp strain during survival on succinate, glutamate and in the absence of exogenous carbon, but not on pyruvate (FIG 4B). Differences in some conditions between strains were non-significant due to variation in individual replicate metabolite values (SUPP FIG 5A). Each carbon source had unique differences between strains (SUPP FIG 5A). Metabolite measurements were not made during survival on glycerol, fructose, or butyrate.

Compared to their individual metabolite levels before anaerobic survival, both strains showed general increases in EMPP, PPP and TCA cycle metabolites in all conditions including pyruvate, likely due to lower carbon utilization during growth arrest (SUPP FIG 6A/6B). These data further support that metabolite accumulation is a general phenotype of transitioning from aerobic growth to anaerobic survival, but that, as survival continues, Xfp prevents further accumulation of upper EMPP and PPP metabolites. Notably, while trends in metabolite differences between the two strains were the same across all conditions except pyruvate, the magnitude of these changes was different for each nutrient condition (SUPP FIG 7). Therefore, different carbon sources likely cause varying levels of carbon influx into the PPP and its related pathways, leading to unique metabolic pressure, potentially explaining the variable importance of Xfp on promoting survival (FIG 4A).

### Anaerobic survival triggers purine degradation and Xfp is essential for maintaining ribonucleotide homeostasis

Because several studies have observed widespread RNA degradation during nutrient starved growth arrest in diverse bacteria (Deutscher, 2003; Himeoka et al., 2022), we hypothesized that release of ribose-5-phosphate during ribonucleotide degradation might explain the accumulation of unlabeled metabolites in the PPP. This notion was bolstered by the fact that studies in mitochondria have shown increased PPP flux and accumulation of ribonucleotides after induction of reductive stress (Wu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2022; Yang, Guo and Li, 2025). Moreover, directly upstream of PA14’s xfp genes are two hypothetical proteins – PA14_17550 and PA14_17570 – with homology to LOG-family proteins and MBL-fold metallo-hydrolases with potential RNA and ribonucleotide degradative functions respectively (Baier and Tokuriki, 2014; Dzurová et al., 2015; Seo et al., 2016).

To test this hypothesis, we measured xanthine – a purine nucleobase degradation product – before and after anaerobic survival under various conditions. After 3 days of anaerobic survival, xanthine levels were ~4 to 32 times higher in both the Δphz and ΔphzΔxfp strains across all conditions compared to their pre-survival levels (FIG 5A). Before and during survival both strains show similar xanthine levels relative to each other, albeit with slight elevation in the ΔphzΔxfp strain generally (FIG 5A, SUPP FIG 8A). Therefore, this data suggests that, irrespective of Xfp activity, anaerobic survival may trigger purine ribonucleotide degradation and xanthine accumulation, in addition to promoting flux into the PPP via ribose-5P. Alternatively, lowered xanthine consumption (via inhibition of ribonucleotide salvage or xanthine degradation to uric acid) could explain these results.

We further hypothesized that buildup of PPP metabolites in the ΔphzΔxfp strain during survival would potentially dysregulate ribonucleotide levels by inhibiting further ribose-5P release during ribonucleotide degradation. After 3 days of anaerobic survival on glucose, ribonucleotides levels were over 4 times higher in the ΔphzΔxfp strain compared to Δphz cells, except for ATP and dUMP (FIG 5B). Ribonucleotide levels were similarly elevated in ΔphzΔxfp cells after 3 days of survival in the absence of an exogenous carbon source, on glutamate, or on succinate compared to Δphz cells (FIG 5C, SUPP FIG 8B). However, loss of xfp did not change ribonucleotide levels during survival on pyruvate (FIG 5C, SUPP FIG 8B), similar to its lack of effect on the accumulation of upper PPP metabolites (FIG 4B). Notably, while trends were similar across conditions, metabolite levels and the effect of xfp mutation occurred at different magnitudes for different nutrient conditions (SUPP FIG 9). This observed increase in ribonucleotide levels in ΔphzΔxfp cells compared to Δphz, cells despite both strains having similar xanthine levels, may suggest faster ribonucleotide polymer (e.g. RNA) breakdown in ΔphzΔxfp cells to form ribonucleotide monomers, but an inhibition of further degradation; alternatively, it may point to increased ribonucleotide biosynthesis. Follow-up studies are needed to distinguish between these possibilities. Regardless, our data suggest that Xfp plays a role in ribonucleotide homeostasis.

To determine if, as seen with PPP and upper EMPP metabolite levels, ribonucleotide accumulation generally occurred upon transition to anaerobic survival, irrespective of xfp, we compared the metabolite levels of each strain during survival to their own levels before survival began. Compared to before survival, ribonucleotide levels only generally increased by 2 times or more in Δphz cells during survival on glucose, but not on other substrates, compared to Δphz cells before survival began (SUPP FIG 10A/10B). In contrast, ribonucleotide levels were generally ~2 to 64 times higher in ΔphzΔxfp cells during survival on all substrates except pyruvate compared to ΔphzΔxfp cells before survival began (SUPP FIG 10C). Both strains individually showed lower ATP levels during survival compared to before on all substrates except for pyruvate and showed large increases upwards of 64 times higher in dUMP levels during survival on pyruvate (SUPP FIG 10B/10C). Therefore, while xanthine accumulation and loss of ATP occur during anaerobic survival irrespective of xfp, ribonucleotide accumulation is generally specific to ΔphzΔxfp cells. As ribonucleotide accumulation is only correlated with PPP metabolite accumulation in ΔphzΔxfp cells, this suggests a role for Xfp in mediating ribonucleotide degradation and/or recycling.

Overall, our data reveal that anaerobic survival triggers purine degradation and PPP metabolite accumulation, necessitating Xfp to maintain homeostasis of these metabolite pools during survival on non-pyruvate carbon sources. We hypothesize that Xfp is necessary because consumption of accumulated PPP metabolites by other pathways would be inhibited under reductive stress, such as the EDP or lower EMPP, or require substantial energetic costs, such as ribonucleotide biosynthesis (FIG 5D). Meanwhile during survival on pyruvate, compared to survival in other nutrient conditions, a relatively higher adenylate charge and/or lower reductive stress conditions could make non-Xfp pathways for metabolite consumption viable, abolishing a need for Xfp activity to maintain metabolic balance. Finally, the increase in AMP and ADP, but not ATP levels in the ΔphzΔxfp strain compared to Δphz cells, suggests that Xfp plays a role in maintaining the cellular energy state as such changes would lead to a lower adenylate charge, which could inhibit functions such as biosynthesis or nutrient transport.

## Discussion

Bacteria are commonly found in growth-arrested states, however, the metabolic networks supporting survival under such conditions are understudied even in model organisms such as P. aeruginosa. Based on studies performed during active growth, P. aeruginosa has been assumed to only catabolize glucose via the EDP (Kohlstedt and Wittmann, 2019; Lessie and Phibbs, 1984), yet here we show that during anaerobic survival it relies on the PPP and a phosphoketolase-dependent pathway, allowing it to mitigate metabolic dysregulation and death. While phosphoketolases occur across the bacterial tree of life, hitherto, their study has focused almost entirely on their role in fermentative metabolisms in obligate anaerobes or their use in natural product generation and synthetic biology (Årsköld et al., 2008; Bogorad, Lin and Liao, 2013; Bruinsma et al., 2023; de Vries and Stouthamer, 1967; Fleige, Kroll and Steinbüchel, 2011; Krüsemann et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2012; Sánchez et al., 2010). Our contribution to bacterial physiology in this study has been to demonstrate that phosphoketolases can also support viability and ribonucleotide homeostasis during oxidant-limited growth arrest in a historically deemed “non-fermentative” or “obligately aerobic” bacterium. Because cancer cell mitochondria experience reductive stress-induced metabolic disruptions similar to those observed in our system, our findings embody the principle of “unity in biochemistry” first articulated by Albert Kluyver over a century ago (Kluyver, 1924).

It is noteworthy that routing of metabolism through the PPP and a phosphoketolase to support anoxic sugar catabolism is shared between fermentative obligate anaerobes, such as Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, or Clostridia species, and P. aeruginosa, which cannot grow fermentatively (Aristilde et al., 2015; Årsköld et al., 2008; de Vries and Stouthamer, 1967; Liu et al., 2012; Sánchez et al., 2010). It reinforces the view that the conceptual divide between “fermenters” and “non-fermenters”, or “obligate aerobes” as P. aeruginosa is commonly but erroneously called, requires reconsideration. Further research investigating whether Xfp-products can be used as electron acceptors would clarify whether P. aeruginosa is capable of Xfp-mediated fermentation decoupled from growth. Moreover, we show P. aeruginosa carries out significant purine degradation during anaerobic survival and reveal an additional role for phosphoketolases in maintaining ribonucleotide homeostasis within this context. Ribonucleotide recycling is a metabolic necessity for various bacteria during growth-arrest, especially during nutrient starvation (Condon, 2007; Deutscher, 2003; Himeoka et al., 2022); yet whether phosphoketolases facilitate this process in other bacteria during growth arrest remains to be determined. However, the importance of phosphoketolases to support PPP flux and therefore generation of ribonucleotide precursors in various species during fermentative of sugars supports the feasibility of such a role (Aristilde et al., 2015; Aristilde, 2017; Årsköld et al., 2008; de Vries and Stouthamer, 1967; Sánchez et al., 2010). Regardless, as research into the biology of growth arrest increases, particularly as induced by oxidant limitation, our ability to identify metabolic strategies that transcend historical growth-oriented classifications and taxonomic distance will improve.

In this vein, we speculate that organisms such as P. aeruginosa may have evolved to survive but not grow under reductive stress. P. aeruginosa prefers non-fermentative easily respirable carbon sources (such as organic acids as opposed to sugars), lacks a few key fermentative genes while containing others, and is unable to use the major NADPH-producing oxidative PPP (Eschbach et al., 2004; Lessie and Phibbs, 1984; McGill et al., 2021). Meanwhile, it also produces phenazines (diffusible electron shuttles) that support non-growth maintenance metabolisms in the absence of terminal electron acceptors (Ciemniecki et al., 2024; Glasser, Kern and Newman, 2014). Our discovery that a phosphoketolase supports anaerobic survival, but not growth, furthers this speculation and demonstrates the multitude of complementary strategies this bacterium uses to survive oxidant limitation. Such a strategy might act to bolster stress tolerance under such conditions, while conserving resources for use upon reintroduction of a terminal electron acceptor.

Under energy limited anaerobic survival conditions, the upper EMPP and PPP may represent a metabolite “reservoir” with Xfp acting as a release valve. The non-oxidative PPP represents the only cyclable central carbon metabolic network in PA14 that produces no reducing equivalents or requires ATP expenditure. Yet, all exits from the PPP (except by way of Xfp) all quickly generate reducing equivalents – lower EMPP – or require ATP expenditure – biosynthesis (FIG 5D) (Kohlstedt and Wittmann, 2019). Extensive use of such cycling is supported by the presence of doubly or triply labelled PPP and upper EMPP metabolites in Δphz cells during anaerobic survival on glucose (FIG 3B, SUPP FIG 3B). Therefore, while Xfp can stimulate energy conservation via substrate phosphorylation during acetate production, we suggest that Xfp’s primary role is to maintain metabolic homeostasis via consumption of accumulated metabolites in the PPP. This conclusion is supported by the lower survival of Δxfp strains on glucose compared to strains lacking only ΔackAΔpta. However, further quantitative flux analysis is required to test this hypothesis. Previous studies in the obligate anaerobe C. acetobutylicum have suggested that phosphoketolase-mediated catabolism of pentoses is faster and requires fewer enzymatic steps than catabolism via other PPP enzymes such as transaldolase (Aristilde et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2012). Therefore, it is plausible that during energy-limited anaerobic survival in P. aeruginosa such a phosphoketolase-based metabolism may act as an enzymatically “cheaper” and faster way to consume PPP metabolites than other pathways.

The dispensability of Xfp during survival on pyruvate but not on other substrates, can also be rationalized (FIG 4A). Pyruvate fermentation does not generate reductive stress because it is redox-balanced (Eschbach et al., 2004; Glasser, Kern and Newman, 2014); it also generates a relatively high adenylate charge ratio and its products (acetate and lactate) can be effluxed to prevent accumulation. Together, these features would enable the cell to maintain balanced PPP metabolism via non-Xfp-mediated pathways (Fig 5D). In contrast, we observed a substantial portion of PPP flux and metabolite accumulation from endogenous carbon stores, one potential source being ribonucleotides. This build-up appears inherent to anaerobic survival, independent of whether Xfp is present, yet Xfp serves to prevent further accumulation and lethality. The survival patterns seen for the parent and xfp mutant in the presence of different carbon sources indicate that during anaerobic survival, carbon metabolism acts as a double-edged sword, with increased catabolic flux fueling energy conservation, and production of biosynthetic precursors, but at the cost of increased reductive stress, leading to increased pressure on the PPP and metabolite accumulation.

A case in point that illustrates this phenomenon is the importance of balanced ribonucleotide recycling, for which the PPP is vital (Condon, 2007; Deutscher, 2003; Himeoka et al., 2022). The PPP produces ribose-5P for ribonucleotide biosynthesis and accepts ribose-5P during ribonucleotide degradation (FIG 5D). During anaerobic survival in P. aeruginosa, purine degradation occurs in an Xfp-independent manner, evidenced by significant increases to xanthine levels (up to ~64 times higher) across strains and conditions, yet we hypothesize that Xfp ensures the cell’s ability to maintain ribonucleotide homeostasis. In fluctuating environments, cells remodel their transcriptome and ribose-5P is generated as a consequence of RNA degradation (Guo and Gross, 2014). Because the rate of ribonucleotide degradation during energy-limited growth-arrest likely outpaces the rate of energetically costly ribonucleotide biosynthesis, ribose-5P accumulation would require Xfp to prevent inhibition of ribonucleotide recycling or other catabolic/anabolic flux through the PPP. Catabolism of carbon sources such as glucose during anaerobic survival would then emphasize this role by causing additional PPP metabolite accumulation on top of accumulation via ribonucleotide degradation. This capability of Xfp to regulate these pathways is supported by the absence of PPP metabolite accumulation despite increases to xanthine and ribonucleotide levels in Δphz cells during anaerobic survival on glucose. While further work is required to determine Xfp’s substrate(s), its homology to a preferentially xylulose-5P degrading phosphoketolase (Petrareanu et al., 2014), and its role in modulating ribonucleotide levels, suggests that xylulose-5P may be a primary substrate in this organism (SUPP FIG1).

In this vein, an intriguing hypothesis is that Xfp’s consumption of ribose-5P, via its equilibration with xylulose-5P, could support redox balance via NAD+ consumption. Degradation of NAD+ and NADP+, releasing AMP and ribose-5P, may represent a strategy to gain increased control over the cellular redox state (Gazzaniga et al., 2009; Gossmann et al., 2012). Lower levels and/or lack of detection of NADH, NADPH, glutathione, and glutathione disulfide in cells surviving on glucose compared to pyruvate may hint at degradation of redox pools as a general cellular strategy to combat reductive stress. However, the pathways to accomplish such degradation are poorly understood in P. aeruginosa.

Alternatively, regulation of PPP metabolite levels by Xfp could avoid energetically costly futile cycling and biosynthesis. During reductive stress and hypoxia, cancer cells have been shown to increase PPP flux and dramatically accumulate ribonucleotides (Wu et al., 2024; Yang, Guo and Li, 2025). In one study the authors suggest that reductive stress deregulates ribonucleotide biosynthesis, leading to de novo purine biosynthesis and ATP consumption (Yang, Guo and Li, 2025). Meanwhile, a separate study found that reductive stress led to ribonucleotide accumulation via the far less costly purine salvage pathway, with the resulting increase in ribonucleotide monophosphates inhibiting de novo biosynthesis preventing further energy expenditure (Wu et al., 2024). Additionally, recent work in the cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus found an Xfp homolog supports survival during light-dark transitions by consuming Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle metabolites to prevent ATP-consuming futile cycling, albeit at the cost of lower carbon fixation (Lu et al., 2023). In tandem with previous studies in C. acetobutylicum suggesting phosphoketolases can act as metabolic “shortcuts” to limit enzymatic costs while hastening pentose catabolism, we speculate that PA14’s Xfp consumption of PPP metabolites could avoid futile and energetically costly biosynthesis (Aristilde et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2023; Servinsky et al., 2012). Such a function could explain why loss of xfp is lethal, with buildup of PPP metabolites forcing biosynthesis, draining ATP and disrupting the adenylate charge. Further testing will determine whether this is in fact the case for PA14 and possibly other bacteria.

In summary, our discovery that Xfp facilitates the maintenance of metabolic homeostasis during anaerobic survival under reductive stress remind us of the adage that “an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure”. Though we have highlighted Xfp’s role in facilitating ribonucleotide homeostasis in P. aeruginosa PA14, given that the PPP and acetyl-P derived compounds are integral to many other anabolic processes, it is possible that Xfp could also play a role in amino acid or fatty acid metabolisms, processes known to support bacterial survival during growth arrest (Bergkessel, Basta and Newman, 2016). Additionally, generation of acetyl-P by Xfp may serve as a vital signaling molecule. The parallels seen in the mitochondria literature, where reductively stressed mitochondria are reported to increase ribonucleotide salvage, amino acid biosynthesis, and lipogenesis (Wu et al., 2024; Yang, Guo and Li, 2025), serve as a powerful reminder of the potential to identify overarching principles of metabolism that span the domains of life as we open our studies of metabolites to include the biology of growth arrest.

### Experimental procedures

#### Strains, culture conditions, and reagents

All strains used can be found in the Supplemental Table 1. All strains were derived from P. aeruginosa UCBPP-PA14 (DKN263, laboratory strain). The Δphz strain lacks the phzA1-G1, phzA2-G2 operons, as well as phzH, phzS, and phzM genes (Meirelles et al., 2021). Cells were streaked from 20% glycerol −80 C freezer stocks onto Difco LB 1.5% agar plates (BD Biosciences) and grown overnight at 37 C. ΔphzΔackAΔpta strain lacked the phzA1-G1 and phzA2-G2 operons as well as the ackA and pta genes (Glasser, Kern and Newman, 2014). The ΔphzΔxfp (this study) strain lacked all genes of the Δphz strain including PA14_17580 encoding a putative phosphoketolase. The ΔphzΔackAΔptaΔxfp (this study) gene lacked all genes of the ΔphzΔackAΔpta strain including PA14_17580.

#### Mutant generation and complementation

All plasmids and primers used can be found in the Supplemental Table 1. Primers were ordered from Integrated DNA technologies. For mutant generation we utilized allelic exchange. Plasmids were synthesized using Gibson assembly (NEB) (Gibson et al., 2009). The plasmid pMQ30 (Shanks et al., 2006) was digested with SmaI, 1 kb regions flanking PA14_17580 were inserted, and the plasmid was transformed into E. coli S17 and conjugated into P. aeruginosa PA14. PA14 conjugates were selected on LB + 70 ug/mL gentamicin and 20 ug/mL of chloramphenicol. Final mutants were then selected on LB + 10% sucrose and no NaCl. Complementation was done by addition of PA14_17580 to the multicloning site of pJM220 (Choi and Schweizer, 2006) under control of a L-rhamnose inducible promoter and transformed into E. coli S17. PA14_17580 was then inserted in trans at the attTn7 site of PA14.

#### Balch tube anaerobic survival assays and viability measurements

Planktonic cultures were made with 7 mL of Difco LB and grown for 20 hours at 37 C at 250 RPM to reach late stationary phase, OD500nm ~ 5. A MOPS minimal media (MM) was used for all experiments (100 mM anhydrous MOPS, 9.3 mM NH4Cl, 3.7 mM KH2PO4, 1 mM MgSO4, 30 uM FeSO4 dissolved in EDTA, and 1x HAquil trace metals mix lacking FeCl3 (Martocello, Morel and McRose, 2019). Cell suspensions for all experiments were prepared by washing stationary phase cells 3x at 10,000 xg for 10 minutes at 4 C with resuspension in MOPS MM, then resuspended to a final volume of 200 uL, the OD500nm measured, and the suspension diluted to an OD500nm of ~75. Cell suspensions were then transferred to an anaerobic Coy Chamber with an atmosphere of N2 and ~1.5–2.5 % H2. Cell suspensions were diluted 5x with N2 sparged MOPS MM. N2 sparged MOPS MM, 250 uL of N2 sparged carbon sources, and 250 uL of cell suspensions were added to Balch tubes to reach a final concentration of OD500nm = 0.75 of cells and 120 mM carbon atoms (ex. 20 mM glucose or 40 mM pyruvate) in a final volume of 5 mL. Balch tubes were then stoppered and crimped before being removed from the Coy Chamber and left to incubate at 30 C at 250 RPM. All Balch tubes, pipettes, and stoppers used were left to passively degas for 5+ days before their use above. Sparging occurred for 30+ minutes in all steps.

To measure CFU/mL of anaerobically surviving cells in Balch tubes, 1 mL syringes with a INSERT GAUGE needle were fully filled and emptied 5 times under a steady flow of N2 to remove oxygen, then inserted into Balch tubes and ~ 200 uL withdrawn and placed in a 96 well plate (Fischer). To confirm no large inputs of oxygen during this, a Balch tube prepared above was given resazurin which is reduced to colorless by cells and re-oxidized by oxygen, turning a bright pink. No pink was seen when inserting or withdrawing media for CFU sampling. Samples were serially-diluted at 10x dilution steps, then 5 uL was platted onto Difco LB + 1.5% agar plates and left to incubate overnight at 37 C before CFUs were counted.

## 96-well potentiostat anaerobic survival assays

Cell suspensions were prepared as in Balch tube experiments, but added to a 96-well electrochemical plate at a final cell OD500nm of 0.75, with 20 mM glucose, set concentrations of phenazine-1-carboxamide (PCN), and MOPS MM to a final volume of 200 uL. PCN was solubilized in DMSO. Samples given 0 uM PCN were given an equal volume of DMSO as a vehicle control. Plates were sealed using both a slit-seal cover (BioChromato #R80.120.00) and an aluminum seal cover (DiversifiedBiotech #ALUM-1000). Each well contained a screen-printed carbon working electrode and counter electrode, and Ag/AgCl reference electrode. The plate was incubated at 33 C without shaking in a custom 96-potentiostat system developed at the National Institute for Materials Science, Japan. Every well’s working electrode was held at a constant 0 mV vs Ag/AgCl. On set days, the aluminum seal was removed and wells mixed by pipetting 150 uL several times. 10 uL was removed and transferred to a 96 well plate and CFUs measured as described above for Balch tube experiments.

### Metabolite extractions

On select days of anaerobic survival in Balch tubes, the full 7 mL cell suspension (OD600 = 0.75) was collected by vacuum filtration onto Whatman 0.22 um nylon filters. Flow-through was collected and frozen at −80 C for downstream measurement of acetate. For collection of intracellular metabolites, filters were dunked upside down in 2 mL cold quenching solution of 40/40/20 methanol/acetonitrile/water (v/v) and incubated at −20 C for 30 minutes. Quenching solution was pipetted up and down over the filter to remove cell debris and the cell suspension was transferred into 2-mL tubes followed by centrifugation at 10,000 g at 4 C for 5 minutes. The supernatant (200 μL) was aliquoted and dried on ice under flow of N2. Dried samples were stored at −80 C until analysis.

### Intracellular metabolite quantification

Intracellular metabolites were quantified based on an established metabolomics protocol using UHPLC (Thermo Fisher Scientific Dionex UltiMate 3000) coupled to high-resolution mass spectrometry (Thermo Fisher Scientific Q Exactive quadrupole-Orbitrap) operating in negative mode (Aristilde et al., 2017). For LC we used an Acquity UPLC BEH C18 Column (particle size 1.7 um, 2.1 mm × 100 mm) maintained at 25 C with an injection volume of 10 uL. The eluents consisted of 97:3 (v/v) water:methanol with 15 mM acetic acid and 10 mM tributylamine (eluent A) and methanol (eluent B)(Aristilde et al., 2017). The flow rate was 0.18 mL min−1 (Aristilde et al., 2017). Relative intensities and the fraction of 13C isotopologues of each metabolite was analyzed using the Metabolomic Analysis and Visualization Engine (MAVEN) software (2011.6.17) (Clasquin, Melamud and Rabinowitz, 2012). IsoCor v2.2.0 was used to correct for natural abundance of 13C (Millard et al., 2019).

### Determination of 13C incorporation into acetate

Extracellular supernatant samples were thawed and diluted 20:1 (sample:acid) with 1M H2SO4. Low pH assured efficient transfer of acetate as acetic acid in the gas phase processes involved in GC-MS analysis. Samples were analyzed with an Agilent 6890 gas chromatograph coupled to a Waters GCT Premier time-of-flight mass spectrometer operating in electron impact positive ion mode. Samples (500 nL) were injected via a split/splitless injector operated in in split mode (20:1) at 250 C. A Phenomenex Focusliner (single taper with wool) (p/n AG0–4680) was installed in the injector. The instrument was tuned to 6000 resolution (m/Δm) and continuous accurate mass calibration was maintained by locking the mass axis to the C4F9+ (218.98508 m/z) ion obtained by continuous admission of perfluorotributylamine via the reference reservoir. Spectra were recorded from 33 to 400 m/z beginning at 2.3 minutes until 10 minutes. Separation of acetate from other components of the sample was achieved on a ZB-FFAP column (Phenomenex, Torrance, CA) 30m × 0.32mm ID × 0.25 microns operated at a constant flow of 0.8 mL/min. Initial column temperature was 100 C for 2 minutes increasing to 124 C at 8 C/min, then increasing to 180 C at 25 C with a final hold for 3 minutes. Acetic acid was eluted at 6.9 minutes. Masslynx and QuanLynx (Version 4.1) software was employed for data processing using peak areas of 60, 61, and 62 m/z for un-labelled, singly 13C-labelled, and doubly 13C-labelled acetic acid, respectively. HCO2+ ions resulting from in-source fragmentation of acetic acid were used to determine labeling at the carboxylate carbon based on the areas of the peaks 45 and 46 m/z for un-labelled and singly 13C labelled fragments, respectively. Ratios of peak areas of labelled to unlabeled ions were used to estimate relative amounts of 13C labelling without further correction.

### Statistical analysis and data visualization

Unpaired two-tailed t-test was applied to determine difference of means between two groups while on-qay analysis of variance (ANOVA) was employed to evaluate difference of means between more than two conditions. Tukey’s honestly significant difference test was used for pairwise comparisons following a significant ANOVA result. P-value threshold for all tests set at 0.05. All data was analyzed and processed in a Python (3.13.2) using Pandas (2.2.3), NumPy (2.1.3), SciPy (1.15.2), and Statsmodels (0.14.4). All plotting was done using Bokeh (2.2.3). Homology between the phosphoketolase amino acid sequences of P. aeruginosa UCBPP-PA14 and P. aeruginosa ATCC 15442 was done using Benchling (https://benchling.com).
